_readme: NEVADA CIVIL DEADLINE RULES -- 10 rows, NRCP 12, 16.1, 33, 34 and 36.
== SOURCE: THE BEST POSITION OF ANY SEEDED JURISDICTION ===============
Read verbatim 2026-08-27 from leg.state.nv.us on a BARE curl -- no
user-agent, no Accept header, no PDF extraction, no browser. Rules and
statutes from ONE publisher, like Minnesota.
AND IT ANSWERS CURRENCY OUTRIGHT, which no other gated source has done.
The NRCP header reads: `[Rev. 4/15/2026] ... ADOPTED BY THE SUPREME COURT
OF NEVADA ... Effective January 1, 1953 and INCLUDING AMENDMENTS THROUGH
OCTOBER 31, 2025` -- a revision stamp AND an explicit amendment cut-off.
NRS chapter 236 stamps `[Rev. 4/15/2026 --2025]` and 236.015's amendment
trail ends at `2023, 1463` with no superseded marker.
Set against the three source traps found the day before -- Utah's `legacy`
hostname that was current anyway, Utah's HTTP 200 with an error-page body,
and Iowa's dated URL that returns identical bytes for every date including
future ones -- Nevada simply tells you what you are reading.
== THE WEEKEND QUESTION ANSWERS ITSELF AT STEP ONE ====================
Second jurisdiction where it does, after Utah. NRCP 6(a)(1)(C) names both
days inside the rollover clause: `if the last day is a Saturday, Sunday,
or legal holiday, the period continues to run until the end of the next
day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday.` No holiday statute
is consulted for the weekend question and there is no statewide-coverage
sub-question. isWeekend() is correct on the rule's own words.
== DAYS ARE DAYS, AND BACKWARD IS REAL ================================
6(a)(1)(B) counts `every day, including intermediate Saturdays, Sundays,
and legal holidays`, so nv_nrcp_6 declares NO short_period_exclusion_days
-- ABSENT, not 0. 6(a)(5) defines backward counting expressly, so the
backward suffix is a real citation rather than the blank NJ/NC/WA/MA/MO/WI
carry. No backward ROW is seeded even so.
== THE CALENDAR IS DERIVED, AND CARRIES THREE TRAPS OF ANALOGY ========
sql/sairnlaw_deadline_calendars_nevada.json, 2026-2031, generated by
tools/gen_nv_calendar.py. SIX years, and the range was CHECKED rather than
copied: Utah stops at 2026 because its holiday statute is superseded
1/1/2027, and Nevada has no pending change.
NRCP 6(a)(6) is a CLEAN SINGLE POINTER -- `Legal holiday means any day set
aside as a legal holiday by NRS 236.015` -- so unlike Utah there is no
in-rule list to reconcile against the statute. That is precisely what made
Utah's Juneteenth question messy, and Nevada cannot drift that way.
THE THREE TRAPS, asserted by the generator rather than trusted:
(1) THERE IS NO COLUMBUS DAY. NRS 236.025 files it under PERIODS OF
OBSERVANCE, not HOLIDAYS. Utah and West Virginia both make it a legal
holiday and the federal calendar has it. THIS IS THE ONLY LATE-
DIRECTION TRAP HERE: encoding it rolls a deadline off a day that is a
normal Nevada business day. Same for Indigenous Peoples Day (236.037)
and Cesar Chavez Day (236.027).
(2) JUNETEENTH IS JUNE 19, A FIXED DATE -- not Utah's third Monday. In
2026 the two states are FOUR DAYS APART: NV 2026-06-19, UT 2026-06-15.
The two were gated a day apart and disagree on one holiday.
(3) NEVADA DAY (31 October, observed the LAST FRIDAY IN OCTOBER) and
FAMILY DAY (the Friday FOLLOWING the fourth Thursday in November). No
other seeded state has either. Missing them reports EARLY, which is
safe, but Family Day is exactly what an analogy-driven calendar drops.
NRS 236.015(3)'s observation shift is BOTH-WAYS but ENUMERATED to five
fixed dates (Jan 1, Jun 19, Jul 4, Nov 11, Dec 25). Complete in practice
-- every other listed day is a weekday rule -- but an ENUMERATION, so a
sixth fixed-date holiday added later would NOT inherit it. IT SPILLS: 1
January 2028 is a Saturday, observed 2027-12-31, so the 2027 calendar
carries 13 days and 2028 carries 11.
== THE WEST VIRGINIA LETTERING TRAP WAS CHECKED AND IS ABSENT =========
WV's Rule 6(e) points at Rule 5(b)(2)(F) while labelling it `(other means
consented to)`, which is the text of its (G). The pointer and the
parenthetical name different subparagraphs, the two readings give opposite
answers on consented electronic service, and this engine refuses both
contested methods rather than choosing. NEVADA'S 6(d) IS WORDED
IDENTICALLY, so NRCP 5(b)(2) was read directly rather than assumed:
(A) handing it to the person
(B) leaving it at the office or dwelling
(C) MAILING it -- `service is complete upon mailing`
(D) LEAVING IT WITH THE COURT CLERK if the person has no known address
(E) the court's electronic filing system, or other ELECTRONIC means
consented to in writing
(F) DELIVERING IT BY ANY OTHER MEANS that the person consented to in
writing
EVERY POINTER MATCHES ITS PARENTHETICAL. Nothing to refuse. Recorded as a
CHECKED negative, because the check is the only thing separating Nevada
from West Virginia here.
== THE EXTENSION: +3, FEDERAL TRIPLE, FEDERAL SEQUENCING ==============
NRCP 6(d): `... service is made under Rule 5(b)(2)(C) (mail), (D) (leaving
with the clerk), or (F) (other means consented to), 3 days are added AFTER
THE PERIOD WOULD OTHERWISE EXPIRE under Rule 6(a).` So nv_nrcp_6_d uses
roll_then_add_then_roll -- the federal sequencing -- read from the words
rather than assumed from the number being three. Ten seeded jurisdictions
use the other order.
NO EXCLUSIVITY CONDITION, unlike Utah's URCP 6(c), whose seven days apply
only to service made `exclusively by mail` and which this engine cannot
express with one service_method field. Nevada's is a plain allowlist.
ELECTRONIC SERVICE UNDER 5(b)(2)(E) TAKES NOTHING, because 6(d) does not
list it. That is the rule, not an omission -- and it is the available
mistake in Nevada practice for the same reason it is in West Virginia and
New York: e-service feels like it should behave like mail.
== WHICH ROWS CARRY THE EXTENSION, AND WHY THE ANSWER ROW DOES NOT =====
READ THIS BEFORE ADDING A ROW. 6(d) reaches a period that runs after
service made UNDER RULE 5. A summons and complaint are served under RULE
4. So the 21-day answer period in 12(a)(1)(A)(i) and the 45-day government
period in 12(a)(2) carry NO service_extension, and every row whose trigger
is a paper served between parties does.
THIS DIVERGES FROM THE FEDERAL SEED IN THIS REPO, DELIBERATELY, AND THE
DIVERGENCE IS FLAGGED RATHER THAN SILENT. `frcp-12a1Ai-answer-after-
service` and `frcp-12a2-united-states-official-capacity` both carry
frcp_6d with an EMPTY note. FRCP 6(d) has the same `under Rule 5(b)(2)`
limitation, and a summons is served under FRCP 4. Minnesota's seed already
records the correct reasoning in terms: `R. 6.01(e) extends a period run
after the service of a notice or other document upon the party; the
summons is served under Rule 4, not Rule 5.` Nevada follows Minnesota.
IF THE FEDERAL ROWS ARE WRONG THEY COMPUTE THREE DAYS LATE, which is the
direction that loses a filing -- raised for a decision rather than fixed
here, because fixing another jurisdiction's rows is not this seed's job.
== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED ===================================
(1) NRCP 15(a)(3). A response to an amended pleading is due `within the
time remaining to respond to the original pleading or within 14 days
after service of the amended pleading, WHICHEVER IS LATER`. One limb is
a COMPUTED PERIOD -- the time remaining on a deadline the engine would
have to derive from a trigger it was never given. That is the Maryland
chained-floor shape. Seeding it as a plain 14-day row would report
EARLY whenever time remains on the original: safe, but it would answer
a question nobody asked.
(2) HOURS-BASED PERIODS. 6(a)(2) states periods in hours with its own
hour-granular rollover; this engine has no hours unit.
(3) 12(a)(3), named in 12(a)(2) as an override, was not read.
(4) Rule 4.2(c)(3)(E), named in 12(a)(1) as an override, was not read.
(5) Appellate rows (NRAP).
(6) NO DEFENDANT FLOOR ON ANY DISCOVERY ROW -- searched 33, 34 and 36 for
`may not seek discovery`, `before the parties have conferred` and `not
be served before`: ZERO hits each. Unlike Ohio, Indiana, Georgia,
Massachusetts, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina and Virginia,
Nevada's discovery periods run purely from service of the request.
Reported as a searched-for absence, not an assumption.
== NOT MODELLED, ALL EARLY, DISCLOSED =================================
6(a)(3)'s clerk's-office INACCESSIBILITY limb is ADDITIONAL to the
Saturday/Sunday/holiday rollover rather than a replacement for it --
Minnesota's 6.01(a)(4) shape, NOT Wisconsin's 801.15(1)(b). That
distinction is what separates a disclosable omission from a blocked
jurisdiction. 5(b)(2)(E) electronic service is complete on sending `but is
NOT EFFECTIVE if the serving party learns that it did not reach the person
to be served` -- a negative condition the engine cannot see, which would
start the period later. Presidentially appointed days of public fast or
thanksgiving under NRS 236.015(1) are ad hoc. Every discovery row and
12(a)(1)(C) carry a stipulation-or-court-order escape the engine cannot
see. All of these can only make a real deadline LATER than the computed
one, so omitting them reports EARLY.
6(a)(4)(A) ends the last day at 11:59 p.m. for electronic filing under the
NEFCR. That does not change the DATE this engine reports; it means a filer
has until 11:59 p.m. on it. Row note, not a mechanism.

rules.label: Answer after service of the summons and complaint (Nevada)

authority.quote: within 21 days after being served with the summons and complaint;
authority.note: TWENTY-ONE DAYS. The quote is the operative limb only; its lead-in reads 'A defendant must serve an answer:' and the sibling limb (ii) covers waiver of service, seeded as its own two rows. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, AND THAT IS A READING RATHER THAN AN OMISSION: NRCP 6(d) reaches a period that runs after service made 'under Rule 5(b)(2)(C), (D), or (F)', and a summons and complaint are served under RULE 4, not Rule 5. Minnesota's seed records the identical reasoning for its own 21-day row. This DIVERGES from the federal seed in this repo, which attaches frcp_6d to FRCP 12(a)(1)(A)(i) with no note recorded — see the file readme; if that federal row is wrong it computes three days LATE. The whole of 12(a)(1) is subject to 'Unless another time is specified by Rule 4.2(c)(3)(E), this rule, or a statute' — two overrides the engine cannot see, neither of which was read.

rules.label: Answer after a timely waiver of service, defendant within the United States (Nevada)

authority.quote: if the defendant has timely waived service under Rule 4.1, within 60 days after the request for a waiver was sent, or within 90 days after the request for a waiver was sent to the defendant outside of the United States.
authority.note: SIXTY DAYS, AND THE CLOCK RUNS FROM WHEN THE REQUEST WAS SENT — not from when it was returned, not from when the waiver was filed, and not from service, which by definition did not happen. Supply the date the waiver request was SENT. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: the period does not run after service at all, so NRCP 6(d) has nothing to attach to; the federal seed reaches the same conclusion on its own waiver rows and says so. The out-of-country limb is a SEPARATE ROW at 90 days, because the choice between them turns on where the request was sent — a fact the caller supplies and the engine cannot derive from a date. Rule 4.1 (the waiver mechanism itself) was not read.

rules.label: Answer after a timely waiver of service, defendant OUTSIDE the United States (Nevada)

authority.quote: if the defendant has timely waived service under Rule 4.1, within 60 days after the request for a waiver was sent, or within 90 days after the request for a waiver was sent to the defendant outside of the United States.
authority.note: NINETY DAYS, from the same sentence as the 60-day domestic limb. Seeded as its own row rather than a variant: picking the wrong one of the two is a THIRTY-day error, so the trigger names say 'outside_us' outright. As with the domestic limb the clock runs from when the request was SENT, and no service extension applies because no service occurred.

rules.label: Answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim (Nevada)

authority.quote: A party must serve an answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim within 21 days after being served with the pleading that states the counterclaim or crossclaim.
authority.note: TWENTY-ONE DAYS. ONE ROW COVERS BOTH DEVICES because the rule states them in one breath with one number — splitting them would invent a distinction the text does not draw. THE SERVICE EXTENSION APPLIES HERE and not on the answer-to-complaint row: the pleading that states a counterclaim or crossclaim is served between parties under Rule 5, which is exactly what NRCP 6(d) reaches.

service_extension.note: NRCP 6(d): three days for service under Rule 5(b)(2)(C) (mail), (D) (leaving with the clerk) or (F) (other means consented to), added AFTER the period would otherwise expire — the federal sequencing, so a second rollover runs. ELECTRONIC SERVICE UNDER 5(b)(2)(E) IS NOT LISTED AND TAKES NOTHING; do not widen this allowlist to email or the e-filing system by analogy to Massachusetts. Nevada's 5(b)(2) lettering was read directly and its pointers match their parentheticals, unlike West Virginia's.

rules.label: Reply to an answer, after an order to reply (Nevada)

authority.quote: A party must serve a reply to an answer within 21 days after being served with an order to reply, unless the order specifies a different time.
authority.note: TWENTY-ONE DAYS, AND THERE IS NO DEADLINE AT ALL WITHOUT AN ORDER. A reply to an answer is not a pleading a party may file at will — NRCP 7(a) allows one only 'if the court orders one'. So this row is reachable only when an order to reply exists, and it runs from service of THAT ORDER, not from the answer. 'UNLESS THE ORDER SPECIFIES A DIFFERENT TIME' is an override the engine cannot see: a specific order always beats this row, and the audit trail names the rule so a reader can tell. The extension applies — a court order is served under Rule 5.

service_extension.note: See the counterclaim row. Electronic service under 5(b)(2)(E) is not listed and takes nothing.

rules.label: Answer by the State of Nevada, a public entity or political subdivision, or their officers and employees — the LATER of two service dates

authority.quote: Unless another time is specified by Rule 12(a)(3) or a statute, the following parties must serve an answer to a complaint, counterclaim, or crossclaim within 45 days after service on the party, or if required service on the Attorney General, whichever date of service is later:
authority.note: FORTY-FIVE DAYS FROM THE LATER OF TWO SERVICE DATES, not from either one alone. Both limbs share ONE count, which is why this is a plain 'later_of' on trigger DATES rather than the resolve_periods shape Georgia needed for O.C.G.A. 9-11-36(a)(2), where the limbs carry different counts. THE ENGINE REFUSES UNLESS BOTH DATES ARE SUPPLIED, because resolving from one limb would be too early whenever the other governs. SERVICE ON THE ATTORNEY GENERAL IS CONDITIONAL — 'IF REQUIRED' — and whether it is required is a question of law the engine does not decide; a caller for whom it was not required should use the ordinary 21-day row instead, not supply the same date twice. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: a complaint on the State is served under Rule 4, not Rule 5 (see the answer-to-complaint row and the file readme). 'Unless another time is specified by Rule 12(a)(3) or a statute' — Rule 12(a)(3) was NOT read, and a Nevada statute may set a different period for a particular entity.

rules.label: Early case conference (Nevada) — 45 days after service of an answer

authority.quote: Attendance at Early Case Conference. Within 45 days after service of an answer, the parties and the attorneys for the parties must confer for the purpose of complying with Rule 16.2(d). The plaintiff may designate the time and place of each meeting, which must be held in the county where the action was filed, unless the parties agree upon a different location. The parties may submit a stipulation and order to continue the time for the case conference for an additional period of not more than 60 days, which the court may, for good cause shown, enter.
authority.note: FORTY-FIVE DAYS AFTER SERVICE OF AN ANSWER. An unusual row to be able to seed at all — most jurisdictions set their case-management clock by court order rather than by rule, so no other seeded state has a conference deadline. THIS IS A DEADLINE TO HOLD A CONFERENCE, NOT TO FILE ANYTHING: the rollover still applies, but 6(a)(4)'s filing cutoffs are irrelevant to it and the date is when the parties must have conferred BY. TWO THINGS IN THE QUOTED TEXT ARE NOT MODELLED AND BOTH RUN LATE-IF-IGNORED IN THE SAFE SENSE: the plaintiff designates the time and place within the period, and the parties may stipulate to continue it 'for an additional period of not more than 60 days' subject to the court's approval — an extension the engine cannot see, which can only make the real date later than this one. Rule 16.2(d), named as the purpose of the conference, was not read. The extension applies — an answer is served under Rule 5.

service_extension.note: See the counterclaim row. Electronic service under 5(b)(2)(E) is not listed and takes nothing.

authority.quote: Time to Respond. The responding party must serve its answers and any objections within 30 days after being served with the interrogatories. A shorter or longer time may be stipulated to under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, matching Nevada's other two discovery rules exactly — 34(b)(2)(A) and 36(a)(3) are both 30, so this jurisdiction has no per-device variation to get wrong (contrast Missouri, where interrogatories and production give 45 and admissions gives 60). NO DEFENDANT FLOOR: Rules 33, 34 and 36 were searched for 'may not seek discovery', 'before the parties have conferred' and 'not be served before' and returned ZERO hits each, so unlike eight other seeded states there is no later_of sibling row. Reported as a searched-for absence, not an assumption. The Rule 29 stipulation and any court order are escapes the engine cannot see.

service_extension.note: See the counterclaim row. Electronic service under 5(b)(2)(E) is not listed and takes nothing.

rules.label: Response to a request for production or inspection (Nevada)

authority.quote: Time to Respond. The party to whom the request is directed must respond in writing within 30 days after being served. A shorter or longer time may be stipulated under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS. This is the deadline for the WRITTEN RESPONSE, not for the production itself — 34(b)(2)(B) has the responding party state that inspection will be permitted, while the request separately 'may specify a reasonable time, place, and manner for the inspection'. That inspection date is chosen by the requesting party and is not computed here. NO DEFENDANT FLOOR (searched; see the Rule 33 row).

service_extension.note: See the counterclaim row. Electronic service under 5(b)(2)(E) is not listed and takes nothing.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission (Nevada) — MISSING IT ADMITS THE MATTER

authority.quote: Time to Respond; Effect of Not Responding. A matter is admitted unless, within 30 days after being served, the party to whom the request is directed serves on the requesting party a written answer or objection addressed to the matter and signed by the party or its attorney. A shorter or longer time for responding may be stipulated to under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF MISSING IT IS AUTOMATIC ADMISSION — the rule is phrased as 'a matter is admitted unless', not as a duty to respond. Unlike Utah, Nevada does NOT require a warning to be printed on the face of the request, so nothing on the document itself will alert the recipient. Thirty here, where Missouri gives 60 for admissions and North Carolina 60 on its second limb: do not reason across states on this rule. NO DEFENDANT FLOOR (searched; see the Rule 33 row).

service_extension.note: See the counterclaim row. Electronic service under 5(b)(2)(E) is not listed and takes nothing.
